**In Praise of the Pencil**

If I get to choose, I want to write about the pencil, because it is one of those objects so ordinary that it has become nearly invisible, and I think invisibility is a shame when the thing in question is quietly astonishing.

Start with the mistake in its name. There is no lead in a pencil and there never was. The core is graphite, a form of carbon, and the confusion dates to the sixteenth century, when a storm reportedly uprooted trees near Borrowdale in the English Lake District and exposed a seam of soft, black, greasy mineral underneath. Local shepherds found it useful for marking their sheep. Nobody knew what it was. It looked a little like lead ore, so people called it "black lead" or, more grandly, *plumbago*—Latin for "acting like lead." The name stuck long after chemists worked out that it had nothing to do with the metal at all. We still say "pencil lead" today, carrying a five-hundred-year-old misidentification around in our pockets.

The Borrowdale deposit turned out to be almost freakishly pure, and for about two centuries it was the only known source of graphite good enough to write with. The English Crown took control of the mine, guarded it, and flooded the shafts between excavations to prevent theft. Graphite was smuggled. People were hanged over it. It is strange to think of a substance we now grind up for children's school supplies once being escorted under armed guard.

The modern pencil owes its existence, oddly, to war. In the 1790s, revolutionary France was cut off from English graphite by blockade. A French officer and inventor named Nicolas-Jacques Conté was asked to find a substitute, and he discovered that if you ground up inferior graphite, mixed it with clay, shaped it into thin rods, and fired it in a kiln, you got a writing core that was not only serviceable but *adjustable*. More clay meant a harder, lighter line; less clay meant a softer, darker one. That is the entire basis of the grading system still printed on pencils today—the H's and B's, the 2B and the 4H. A whole vocabulary of shading was born because one country couldn't buy from another.

Then there is the yellow. Most pencils in North America are painted yellow, and there is a reason for it, though it is a marketing reason rather than a practical one. In 1889, at the Paris World's Fair, an Austro-Hungarian company introduced a luxury pencil called the Koh-I-Noor, named after the famous diamond. The best graphite of the day came from China, and yellow was associated with Chinese imperial dignity, so the company painted its pencils yellow to signal quality and provenance. The pencil was a sensation. Competitors copied the color, and within a few decades yellow simply meant "pencil." Nothing about the wood or the graphite requires it. It is a century-old advertisement that we have all agreed to stop noticing.

Henry David Thoreau, of all people, was a pencil maker. His family ran a pencil business in Concord, Massachusetts, and before he went off to live deliberately beside a pond, he spent years improving the firm's product—refining the grinding of graphite, experimenting with clay ratios, possibly developing a better way to drill the cores into the wood. Thoreau pencils were considered among the finest in America. I find it wonderful that the man who wrote "Simplify, simplify" spent a serious portion of his life on the engineering of a small cylinder of cedar.

The physics of why a pencil works at all is worth a moment. Graphite is carbon arranged in flat sheets, each sheet a honeycomb of atoms bonded very tightly to one another. But the sheets are bonded to *each other* only weakly. They slide. When you drag a pencil across paper, the fibers of the page catch the outer layers and peel them off, a few atoms thick, leaving them behind as a mark. That is the whole trick. You are shearing a crystal, one sheet at a time, and calling it handwriting. A diamond is the same element arranged differently, with every atom locked to its neighbors in three dimensions, which is why you can write with one and not the other.

The eraser came late and came with a lawsuit. In 1858 an American named Hymen Lipman patented a pencil with a rubber plug set into one end. He sold the patent for a considerable sum, and the buyer tried to enforce it against competitors, but the Supreme Court eventually threw it out, ruling that sticking two existing things together did not make a new invention. The decision has been cited in patent law ever since. The pink cap on your pencil is, in a small way, a landmark of intellectual property.

What I like most about the pencil, though, is not its history but its character. A pencil is honest about being temporary. Ink commits; graphite proposes. Everything written in pencil carries an implicit *for now*. Architects draft in it, composers sketch in it, students hedge in it. It is the medium of the first attempt, the crossed-out line, the margin note that says *check this*. It is also the only writing instrument that visibly consumes itself in use. A pen runs dry invisibly; a pencil gets shorter, and you watch it happen. By the end, it is a stub you hold with three fingers, and then it is gone, distributed across a hundred pages as a faint gray dust. There is something almost moral in that—an object that gives itself away entirely, that leaves nothing behind but what it said.

A pencil needs no power, no cartridge, no software update. It writes upside down and underwater and in the cold. It has not meaningfully changed since Conté fired his first kiln. The hexagonal ones don't roll off the desk. And it is, still, one of the cheapest things you can buy that lets you make a thought visible to someone else.

I think that is worth a thousand words. It has quietly earned more.
